Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> An analysis of the U.S. federal budget for fiscal year 2023, which ended on September 30, 2023, revealed a deficit of nearly $1.7 trillion. [1, 3, 7] The primary driver for the deficit's growth compared to the previous year was a significant decline in revenues, which fell by approximately $457 billion, or 9.3%. [1, 3] This decrease was largely attributed to a 17% drop in individual income tax collections. Key factors contributing to this revenue shortfall included lower capital gains realizations following a downturn in the stock and housing markets, a presidentially-authorized delay in tax filing deadlines for most of California due to severe weather, and a surge in unexpectedly high, and potentially fraudulent, claims for the pandemic-era Employee Retention Tax Credit. [1] <2> Hours before the midnight deadline, the U.S. Congress passed a temporary 45-day funding bill on September 30, 2023, averting a government shutdown. [1, 2, 6] The bill, which secured government funding until November 17, included $16 billion in disaster relief but notably excluded aid for Ukraine. [1, 6] To ensure its passage, House Speaker Kevin McCarthy bypassed dissent from hardline members of his own party and relied on significant support from Democrats; more Democrats than Republicans ultimately voted for the measure. [5, 6] This bipartisan maneuver was acknowledged by McCarthy as a political risk that could prompt a challenge to his leadership position. [1] <3> The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) announced in its Monthly Budget Review that the U.S. government recorded an estimated budget surplus of $90 billion for August 2023. [1] This contributed to a cumulative federal budget deficit of $1.5 trillion for the first 11 months of fiscal year 2023 (from October 2022 through August 2023). [1, 2] The surplus in August was largely influenced by a significant reduction in outlays recorded for the student loan program following a Supreme Court ruling. [1] Without this reduction, outlays in August 2023 would have been comparable to the previous year. [1] The cumulative deficit through August 2023 was $0.6 trillion more than the deficit recorded during the same period in the prior fiscal year. [2] <4> On August 31, 2023, the White House formally requested that Congress approve a short-term spending bill, known as a continuing resolution, to prevent a partial government shutdown. [2] The fiscal year was scheduled to conclude on September 30, and an official from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) stated it was clear a temporary measure would be necessary to give lawmakers more time to negotiate and finalize the individual annual appropriations bills for the 2024 fiscal year. [2] The OMB offered Congress technical assistance to help avert significant disruptions to government services that would occur if funding lapsed on October 1. [2] The request came amid political pressure on then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy from conservative members of his party regarding an impeachment inquiry into President Biden. [2] <5> The U.S. Department of the Treasury reported a federal budget deficit of $221 billion for July 2023. For the first ten months of the fiscal year 2023, which began on October 1, 2022, the cumulative deficit was $1.614 trillion. According to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the deficit for this ten-month period was more than double the shortfall recorded during the same period in the previous fiscal year. The CBO noted that outlays for July 2023 were lower than they might have been because certain payments due on July 1, 2023, a Saturday, were processed in June. Without such timing shifts, the CBO estimated the deficit for July 2023 would have been $307 billion. <6> In its Monthly Budget Review for July 2023, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) updated its projection for the fiscal year 2023 budget deficit to $1.7 trillion. [3, 4] This figure represents an increase of approximately $200 billion from the $1.5 trillion deficit that the CBO had projected in May 2023. [3, 4] The revision was based on 10 months of actual budget data for the fiscal year and preliminary estimates for the remaining months. [4] The CBO noted that while both revenues and outlays were anticipated to be lower than the May projections, the decrease in revenues was more significant, leading to the larger projected deficit. [4] <7> On August 1, 2023, Fitch Ratings downgraded the United States' long-term foreign-currency issuer default rating to 'AA+' from 'AAA'. The agency attributed the downgrade to an expected fiscal deterioration over the next three years, a high and growing general government debt burden, and a noted "erosion of governance" compared to other highly-rated countries. This erosion was characterized by a steady deterioration over the last 20 years, manifested in repeated political standoffs over the debt limit. A senior director at Fitch later elaborated that growing political polarization, including events like the January 6th insurrection, contributed to this view on governance. The U.S. Treasury Secretary, Janet Yellen, publicly disagreed with the decision, calling it "arbitrary and based on outdated data." <8> The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) released its 2023 Long-Term Budget Outlook on June 28, 2023, which projects the nation's fiscal future over the next three decades under current law. [1] The report indicates that federal debt held by the public is projected to rise from 98 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at the end of fiscal year 2023 to 181 percent by 2053. [2] It also projects that the budget deficit will grow from 5.8 percent of GDP in 2023 to 10.0 percent in 2053. [2, 3] This projected increase in deficits and debt is attributed to spending, particularly on retirement, healthcare, and net interest, growing more rapidly than revenue. [1] The CBO's projections are based on their May 2023 baseline but also incorporate the budgetary effects of the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, which was enacted on June 3, 2023. [2, 3] Compared to the previous year's outlook, the debt projection for 2052 is nine percentage points lower. [3, 4] <9> The U.S. Department of the Treasury reported a budget deficit of $240 billion for May 2023. For the first eight months of the fiscal year, which began in October 2022, the cumulative deficit reached approximately $1.16 trillion. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) offered a slightly different estimate, placing the deficit for the same eight-month period at $1.2 trillion. The CBO noted that this figure would have been $1.224 trillion if not for certain payment timing shifts, bringing its adjusted figure closer to the Treasury's reported $1.161 trillion.

[11] Meanwhile, the income generated from its portfolio of longer-term securities, locked in at lower rates, did not keep pace. [1, 2] This amount represents a $47 billion increase compared to the deficit recorded during the same two-month period in the prior fiscal year. [1, 2] The rise in the deficit was a result of federal outlays increasing more significantly than the growth in revenues. [1] While revenues saw a substantial increase of $108 billion, or 19 percent, outlays rose by an even greater margin of $155 billion, or 17 percent. [1] The U.S. federal fiscal year runs from October 1 to September 30. <2> The U.S. Department of the Treasury reported a federal budget deficit of $66.6 billion for October 2023. [8] This official figure was slightly lower than an earlier estimate from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), which had projected the deficit to be $67 billion. [4] The Treasury's report indicated that receipts for the month were $403.4 billion while outlays were $470.0 billion. [8] The official Monthly Treasury Statement containing these final figures was released on November 13, 2023. [8] <3> In November 2023, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) announced its estimate that the U.S. government incurred a deficit of $65 billion for October 2023, the first month of fiscal year 2024. [1] This figure represents a $23 billion reduction from the deficit recorded in October 2022. [1] According to the CBO's report, both revenues and outlays were higher in October 2023 than in the previous year, but the increase in revenues surpassed the increase in outlays. [1] Revenues were significantly boosted by the deferral of certain individual and corporate income tax payments into October. [1] It was also noted that payment timing shifts affected the deficit calculations; had it not been for these shifts, the October 2023 deficit would have been an estimated $137 billion. [1] <4> A retrospective analysis of the U.S. federal government's fiscal year 2023, which ran from October 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023, confirmed a dramatic drop in remittances from the Federal Reserve to the U.S. Treasury. In fiscal year 2022, the Fed contributed a net income of $58.8 billion, but in 2023, its expenses surpassed earnings by $114.3 billion, effectively halting these payments. [2, 11] This negative turnaround was primarily caused by the Federal Reserve's own monetary policy actions to combat inflation. [10] As the Fed aggressively raised short-term interest rates, its interest expenses—particularly payments on bank reserves and reverse repurchase agreements—soared, increasing by $178.7 billion from the previous year. [11] Meanwhile, the income generated from its portfolio of longer-term securities, locked in at lower rates, did not keep pace. [3, 10] This shift from profit to loss began in September 2022 and resulted in the Fed recording a 'deferred asset,' which represents the earnings it must generate before resuming Treasury remittances. [10, 11] The absence of these funds was a contributing factor to the overall federal budget deficit, which reached nearly $1.7 trillion in fiscal year 2023. This figure is based on estimated outlays of $6.1 trillion and revenues of $4.4 trillion. The fiscal year 2022 deficit was itself a significant reduction from the COVID-19 pandemic-era high of $2.8 trillion in 2021. [8] This substantial revenue shortfall contributed significantly to the widening budget deficit. [1, 3, 7] The primary driver for the deficit's growth compared to the previous year was a significant decline in revenues, which fell by approximately $457 billion, or 9.3%. [1, 3] This decrease was largely attributed to a 17% drop in individual income tax collections. [1, 2, 6] The bill, which secured government funding until November 17, included $16 billion in disaster relief but notably excluded aid for Ukraine. [1, 6] To ensure its passage, House Speaker Kevin McCarthy bypassed dissent from hardline members of his own party and relied on significant support from Democrats; more Democrats than Republicans ultimately voted for the measure. [5, 6] This bipartisan maneuver was acknowledged by McCarthy as a political risk that could prompt a challenge to his leadership position. The agency stated that a shutdown would highlight the weakness of U.S. institutional and governance strength compared to other Aaa-rated nations. Moody's further noted that such an event would underscore the constraints that escalating political polarization place on fiscal policymaking. This warning came at a time of deteriorating debt affordability driven by persistent fiscal deficits and higher interest rates. Subsequently, on November 10, 2023, Moody's lowered the U.S. credit outlook from "stable" to "negative," citing continued political polarization and the rising risks to the nation's fiscal strength without a clear plan to address the large deficits. <10> The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) announced in its Monthly Budget Review that the U.S. government recorded an estimated budget surplus of $90 billion for August 2023. [1] This contributed to a cumulative federal budget deficit of $1.5 trillion for the first 11 months of fiscal year 2023 (from October 2022 through August 2023). [1, 2] The surplus in August was largely influenced by a significant reduction in outlays recorded for the student loan program following a Supreme Court ruling. [1] Without this reduction, outlays in August 2023 would have been comparable to the previous year. [1] The cumulative deficit through August 2023 was $0.6 trillion more than the deficit recorded during the same period in the prior fiscal year. [2]
